S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.

subtypes.Intrusive Memories: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Distressing Dreams: Recurrent distressing dreams in which the content and/or affect of the dream are related to the traumatic event.
subtypes.Dissociative Reactions (Flashbacks): Dissociative reactions (e.g., flashbacks) in which the individual feels or acts as if the traumatic event were recurring.
subtypes.Psychological Distress at Cues: Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Physiological Reactions to Cues: Marked physiological reactions to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.

subtypes.Internal Avoidance: Efforts to avoid distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about or closely associated with the traumatic event.
subtypes.External Avoidance: Efforts to avoid external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations) that arouse distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).

subtypes.Anhedonia for Happiness: Unable to feel happiness or joy even when good things happen.
subtypes.Lack of Satisfaction: Unable to experience satisfaction or pride even after achieving something good.
subtypes.Inability to Feel Love: Feeling numb to love or affection towards family or lovers.
subtypes.Emotional Numbness: A state where the mind feels empty and nothing is felt, as if all positive emotions are blocked.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.

subtypes.Impulsive Anger: Sudden explosions of anger for trivial reasons or no clear reason.
subtypes.Verbal Aggression: Attacking others with shouting, cursing, or blame without holding back.
subtypes.Physical Aggression: Physically attacking people or throwing/breaking objects.
subtypes.Chronic Irritability: A state where nerves are always sharp and sensitive, ready to explode at the slightest touch.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.

subtypes.Auditory Startle: Startling excessively and flinching physically at sudden noises.
subtypes.Tactile Startle: Being extremely startled by unexpected physical contact.
subtypes.Visual Startle: Being greatly startled and wary of sudden appearances of people or rapid movements.
subtypes.Slow Recovery: Heart pounding and trembling for a long time after being startled, not calming down easily.

S082.name: Depersonalization_Derealization
S082.description: Altered sense of the reality of one's self or surroundings after a traumatic event.

subtypes.Depersonalization: Feeling detached from one's own body or mental processes, as if being an outside observer.
subtypes.Derealization: The surrounding environment feels unreal, dreamlike, distant, or distorted.
subtypes.Time Distortion: Time feels like it has stopped during the traumatic moment, or is perceived as moving extremely slowly or quickly.

symptom.disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that emerges within days of exposure to a traumatic event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, either directly, as a witness, or through close association. It is characterized by a cluster of intrusive, negative mood, dissociative, avoidance, and arousal symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month after the trauma, with associated functional impairment or significant distress. Clinically, ASD often presents as a rapid-onset disturbance in emotional regulation and sense of self or reality, sometimes with marked autonomic reactivity and difficulty engaging in normal roles. It is distinguished from posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) primarily by its shorter duration and more prominent dissociative features early on, and it may represent a risk state for later development of PTSD if symptoms persist or worsen.

patient.personality: Miguel is a structured, data-driven and compassionate supervisor who thrives on mentoring others, staying socially engaged, and taking on multiple community and cultural commitments at once.
patient.stressor: Miguel was closing his store late one evening when an armed robbery occurred; he was in the back office reconciling budgets while two of his younger employees were held at gunpoint on the sales floor, and he briefly confronted the assailant when trying to reach them. The police arrived quickly and no one was physically harmed, but Miguel stayed to give statements, help review security footage, and support his shaken staff, all while privately replaying the moment he stepped into the gunman’s path and believing he might have gotten his team killed. Over the next several days, he pushed himself to keep the store running, attended corporate debriefings, and tried to model calm leadership, but he found he could not function normally at work or at home, avoiding the store entrance and delegating all closing duties to others while becoming visibly on edge in any situation that even faintly reminded him of the incident. When he startled so dramatically at a minor stockroom noise that he knocked over a display and frightened a new employee to tears, his district manager insisted he take leave and see a mental health professional, which Miguel reluctantly agreed to after realizing he could no longer trust himself to keep his staff or customers feeling safe.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since the robbery at the store, I jump out of my skin at the smallest sound or movement.”

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
S069.manifestation: All day and especially when I try to sleep, I keep seeing that exact second when I stepped out of the office and the gun was pointed at my kids on the floor, and it just slams into my head like a movie I can’t shut off—my chest tightens, my hands sweat, and I’m right back there instead of at home or in my bed.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.
S070.manifestation: I’m doing everything I can to not think about it—I avoid walking past the store entrance, I won’t go near the back office at night, I turn off the news if anything about crime comes on, and if my wife or anyone at church tries to ask how I’m doing, I change the subject because even talking about it makes me feel like I’m going to lose it.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).
S076.manifestation: Since the robbery, even when my daughter shows me a good grade or my team texts something funny in our group chat, I just feel flat and disconnected, like I’m watching someone else’s life and can’t access any real joy or warmth.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.
S077.manifestation: I’ve been snapping at everyone over nothing—raising my voice at my staff for minor mistakes, barking at my wife for asking simple questions, and then feeling horrified afterward because it’s like there’s no buffer between me and this anger that comes out of nowhere.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.
S080.manifestation: Now the tiniest noise—a carton dropped in the stockroom, a car backfiring outside, my son walking into the room too quickly—makes me jump out of my skin, my heart pounding so hard I feel shaky for several minutes before I can even pretend to act normal again.

S082.name: Depersonalization_Derealization
S082.description: Altered sense of the reality of one's self or surroundings after a traumatic event.
S082.manifestation: Several times a day, especially when I walk through the mall or sit in meetings, everything around me goes kind of hazy and far away, like I’m underwater or watching myself from across the room, and I feel like I’m not really there, just going through the motions on autopilot.
